title: Anthropic Says Its AI Model Cut AMD Chip Switch to Three Days
content:
Anthropic Says Its AI Model Cut AMD Chip Switch to Three Days. Why it Could be a Challenge to Nvidia
Anthropic said its own artificial intelligence model helped get Claude running on AMD chips in three days, accelerating work that previously required months.
The claim, presented to investors ahead of Anthropic's proposed initial public offering, suggests AI coding tools could reduce the engineering burden that makes switching chip suppliers difficult. However, the three-day result covers a specific workload, rather than a complete migration of Claude's training and operations.
Tom Brown, Anthropic's co-founder and chief compute officer, said the company used its Mythos model to handle the transition after beginning work with AMD GPUs this year. According to the presentation, Mythos wrote or ported nearly all the necessary kernels, the specialized software routines that execute calculations on chips. "It got Claude running on AMD in just three days with basically no human intervention," Brown said in the investor presentation.
The approximately three-day timeline refers to bringing up prompt processing for one Anthropic model on AMD MI355X GPUs at a useful performance level. Prompt processing is the stage in which a model reads and processes input before generating its response.
The reported acceleration addresses a significant obstacle for Nvidia's competitors. CUDA provides the software infrastructure developers use to put Nvidia GPUs to work. Companies that have built their systems around that ecosystem can face substantial engineering costs when adapting their software to another supplier's hardware.
If AI can perform more of that adaptation, customers could gain flexibility to choose chips based on availability, performance and cost. Anthropic says it has spent years building that flexibility. Its IPO materials describe a computing architecture spanning four chip families: Nvidia GPUs, AMD GPUs, Amazon Web Services Trainium chips and Google's tensor processing units.
The company treats capacity across its partners as a shared pool, allocating computing resources to research, model development, customer services and internal AI use. Its investor fact sheet identifies both its multiple-chip architecture and research breakthroughs as foundations of that approach.
The strategy could become increasingly important as demand for AI computing grows. Different workloads have different requirements, and access to multiple suppliers gives Anthropic more options when adding capacity or deciding where to run particular tasks.
Anthropic also describes research advances as "compute multipliers," improvements intended to extract more capability from existing hardware. The company's longer-term ambition includes having Claude help discover further efficiency gains. That remains an objective, rather than proof of autonomous recursive self-improvement.

report.summary: Anthropic says its Mythos AI model ported Claude's prompt processing to AMD MI355X GPUs in three days, hinting AI could ease chip-switching and challenge Nvidia's CUDA moat.
report.background: Nvidia's CUDA software ecosystem has long been a major barrier for competitors. Developers build AI systems around CUDA libraries and kernels, so moving to AMD GPUs or custom chips like AWS Trainium or Google TPUs often requires months of specialized engineering. That lock-in helps Nvidia preserve its dominant position in AI computing. Anthropic, which relies heavily on compute for training and serving Claude, has been building a multi-chip architecture spanning Nvidia, AMD, AWS, and Google hardware. Ahead of a proposed IPO, the company is presenting its compute strategy and research advances as key advantages. The claim that an internal AI model, Mythos, automated most kernel porting work is meant to show that AI coding tools could reduce switching costs and give AI companies more leverage over chip suppliers.
key_points: Anthropic used its Mythos model to write or port nearly all the specialized kernels needed to get Claude running on AMD MI355X GPUs. Co-founder Tom Brown said the work took about three days with basically no human intervention, compared with months of typical engineering effort.

The result covers prompt processing for one Anthropic model at useful performance, not a full migration of Claude's training and operations. That narrow scope matters: porting production workloads across chip families remains far more complex than bringing up one workload.

The claim directly targets Nvidia's CUDA moat. If AI tools can automate more kernel adaptation, customers could choose chips based on availability, performance, and cost rather than software lock-in, potentially benefiting AMD and custom silicon vendors.

Anthropic says it has spent years building a multi-chip architecture spanning Nvidia GPUs, AMD GPUs, AWS Trainium, and Google TPUs. It treats capacity across partners as a shared pool for research, model development, customer services, and internal AI use.

The disclosure comes ahead of Anthropic's proposed IPO and is presented to investors as evidence of its compute flexibility. Anthropic also describes research advances as 'compute multipliers' that extract more capability from existing hardware, though autonomous self-improvement remains an ambition, not a proven capability.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Anthropic's claim is a signal that AI-assisted coding could gradually erode Nvidia's CUDA advantage by lowering the cost of porting software to AMD and custom chips. That could intensify competition among chip suppliers and give large AI companies more bargaining power. For developers, the shift may reduce demand for low-level kernel engineering while raising the value of AI agents that can automate hardware-specific optimization. For regular users, the eventual effect could be more competition, better hardware availability, and potentially lower AI inference costs, though not immediately. The caveat is scope: a three-day prompt-processing bring-up is not a full production migration, so Nvidia's software ecosystem remains a powerful moat for now.
report.tools: To follow the kernel-porting trend, watch OpenAI Triton, MLIR, and Apache TVM for compiler-based hardware abstraction; AMD's ROCm and HIP for open GPU programming; and AI coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenHands for automating low-level code translation. Anthropic's Mythos model is not publicly available, but the broader space of AI-assisted kernel generation and performance tuning is worth tracking.
